## What you build today

The passive tail, cut to the shape your simulation produced and mounted on its
rod, plus the foam housing that protects the robot and keeps it afloat.

## Before you arrive

| | |
|---|---|
| **Parts** | Carbon sheet and tail rod, foam stock (XPS or closed-cell PE), epoxy |
| **Tools** | Foam cutter, scalpel |
| **Bring** | Your Module 6 tail geometry, printed 1:1 |

## Trailing edge holder
Insert part on tube.

## Housing

Use a foam cutter to cut an exterior housing for the FAAV. This is an important
step for external tests: it adds a layer of protection and ensures the FAAV
floats. Leave space for GPS and antenna insertions if you are using them.

To keep the FAAV level when floating --- which helps visibility and getting it
out of the water --- it is recommended to put a certain amount of foam on the
tail.

### Choosing a foam

Various foams have been tested, with tradeoffs:

| Foam | Floatability | Absorption | Impact behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| Extruded polystyrene (XPS) | Best, low density | Zero | Relatively brittle; little help damping landings |
| Closed-cell polyethylene (PE) | Decent, relatively low density | Light | Much more compliant; usable as protection |

If someone ever has time, a multi-material housing could have its use cases.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Check solvent compatibility before painting or gluing foam

Some foams are very sensitive to solvents. Epoxy is inert and can act as glue.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Checkpoint --- TA sign-off

Tail mounted and aligned, housing fitted with clearance for the wings through
the full flap cycle, and the assembled robot floating level in the test tank.
:::
